div.p: The Detection Confidence Tool answers, for a nuclide and a shielding configuration, either "how much activity could be present without my having seen it?" or "how far away could the source be and still be detected?". Unlike the Simple MDA tool, which looks at a single gamma line, this tool can combine several lines of the same nuclide into one limit, and it lets you fit shielding alongside.

Each gamma line gets its own row showing a Currie-style limit computed from the counts in that region alone. Ticking "Use for multi-peak" on a row adds that line to the combined deconvolution limit, which fits peaks of the expected shape at a range of trial activities and finds where the fit becomes inconsistent with the data. The chart shows that scan.
Three options sound similar and are routinely confused; they answer different questions and are chosen independently.

ul.li: Cont. Norm (per row) — where the knowledge of the background under that peak comes from. Covered in detail below.

Measurement — which measurement the limit describes. Current spectrum bounds the signal in the spectrum you have. Background reference asserts this spectrum is signal-free and predicts what a future measurement of the entered length could detect. The reference counts and the projected measurement are scored together, sharing one continuum, so the reference's own counting statistics are carried into the answer rather than wished away. The result is a predicted median sensitivity, not a bound on the loaded spectrum, and never worded as one. It is a good median while the entered time is around the reference's or shorter; reaching much further it reads optimistic, for the reason given under "Measurement time" below.

Limit — which quantity to report. Upper limit is a one-sided bound: "less than U at this confidence". Central interval is two-sided: "between L and U". They use different thresholds on the statistic, so the choice is explicit rather than guessed. Note the two roots found at a one-sided threshold do not form a central interval — together they cover only about 2×CL−1, so two 95% one-sided bounds make roughly a 90% central interval. When that happens the result says so instead of calling it an interval. And on a spectrum with no signal a central interval usually runs into the physical boundary at zero, leaving only the upper endpoint; that is reported as "between 0 and U", which is not a one-sided upper limit at the same confidence — the endpoint sits at a higher threshold.

div.p: The mechanical difference is small; the difference in what you are claiming is not. It comes down to where the knowledge of the background comes from.

ul.li: Floating infers the background from the same channels that might contain the signal. You assert nothing about the neighbourhood. The question it answers is: "given only this window, and no prior knowledge of where the continuum sits, how much signal is consistent with the data?"

Anchored by side channels measures the background next door and imports it. You assert that the shoulders contain no signal and that the continuum runs straight through them into the region. The question becomes: "given the continuum is what the neighbours say it is, how much signal is consistent with the region?"

div.p: That leads to a difference worth knowing: Floating responds to peak shape, while anchoring also responds to level. Under Floating a broad or uniform elevation across the region is absorbed into the continuum, so only genuinely peak-shaped excess counts as signal. When anchored, a region that simply sits higher than its shoulders is signal, whether or not it looks Gaussian. Floating is the stricter test of "is that actually a peak?"

The failure modes are not symmetric. Floating errs toward wider limits — it can quietly absorb real signal into the continuum, so it may understate a detection. That holds while the continuum model fits; where it cannot — a curved background across a wide region — Floating overstates your confidence instead, and the paragraph below explains when. Anchoring errs toward wrong limits in either direction if its assumption fails: a neighbouring line, a Compton edge, a step, or curvature across the window biases the shoulders, and the limit moves with them.

Adding signal-free channels can only add information, so anchoring reliably has the smaller uncertainty — but not necessarily the smaller limit, since the central value moves too, depending on whether the shoulders happen to sit high or low. A narrower number is not automatically a better one.

In practice: default to Floating — it is the best-validated mode and the defensible number when someone asks what you assumed. Reach for the side channels when the region is clean and smooth for several FWHM either side, you have actually looked at the shoulders rather than trusting them, and the extra sensitivity is worth the assertion. Never anchor with an interfering line within a few FWHM: that is exactly the case where the shoulders mislead and the method cannot notice. Note also that anchoring forces a linear continuum, since four-plus-four side channels barely determine an offset and a slope. Floating does not escape that by itself — its default continuum is a straight line too — but Floating can be given a quadratic continuum, which is the option to reach for when the region visibly curves.
Anchoring is not a "fixed" continuum: the shoulders' own counting uncertainty is carried in the likelihood, so a weak anchor honestly widens the limit rather than pretending the continuum is known.

The deconvolution method models the background under the peak as a straight line by default. Where the true background curves noticeably across the region — wide regions, and so lower-resolution detectors — a straight line cannot follow it, and the limit comes out optimistic; the effect grows with counting time. For HPGe, regions are narrow enough that this is negligible. If the background visibly curves across your region, select the Quadratic continuum type, or narrow the region.

The Meas. time control is the dwell you are asking about, and appears when the measurement is a background reference. The reference counts are left alone and this becomes the exposure of the predicted future measurement, so a short background gives a correspondingly weaker prediction. The per-row Currie limits are projected to the same dwell, so the two numbers on screen always describe the same planned measurement.

The two get there by different routes, though, and only one of them scales counts. Writing k for the entered time divided by the loaded spectrum's, the projected Currie limits predict the typical future limit well — within 4% of what the dwell delivered, measured across a 64-fold span of k on a real 11.5 hour background — but understate the spread around that prediction, because scaling counts asserts the background's rate is known exactly. The measured scatter ran about 1.6× wider than implied at k = 1 and about 4× wider at k = 16.

The deconvolution prediction does not scale counts and carries the reference's statistics honestly, but the future measurement has not been taken, so it stands in a spectrum holding exactly the counts it expects — perfectly smooth, with no measurement noise at all. Measured against the same calculation re-run with a real future measurement in place of that stand-in, the stand-in itself is sound: where the continuum under the region really is the straight line the model fits, the two agree to a few percent with no trend in k, over four decades of counts under the peak.

On a real region that agreement holds while k is around one or below — on an 11.5 hour background it measured 1.04 at k = 0.25 and 0.96 at k = 1 — and then falls away, to 0.70 at k = 4 and 0.63 at k = 16, the prediction reading tighter than the real analysis by that factor. That is not the stand-in; it is the continuum, described next, and the reason the wording below is worth acting on when a long dwell is being planned.

Where a predicted sensitivity and a real analysis of the same region do disagree, the usual cause is the continuum. A region whose true shape the straight line cannot follow — noticeable curvature, or an unmodelled line inside the region — drives the limit tighter than it should be, and more so the longer the measurement, because the mis-fit grows with counting time while the counting noise only grows as its square root. This affects an ordinary single-spectrum limit just as much as a prediction. If a region looks suspiciously sensitive, check that the continuum under the peak is actually straight over the width you have chosen, and narrow the region if it is not.

The confidence levels offered include the central-normal probabilities for 1σ through 5σ — 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%, 99.9937%, 99.999943% — but they are applied as one-sided confidence levels unless you select a central interval. They are offered because they are familiar numbers, not because the limit is a multiple of any sigma. The label above the selector says which of the two is in force.

The chart's vertical axis, and the "best χ2" line below it, show a quantity labelled χ2. That name is kept for continuity, but the quantity is the Cash statistic — a Poisson deviance, 2·∑(E − n + n·ln(n/E)), summed once per channel (Cash 1979). It is a genuine likelihood ratio, not a Pearson or modified-Neyman χ2, and it is used because it has no variance bias and needs no variance floor for empty channels — exactly the regime a detection limit lives in.

Only differences of it between trial activities are meaningful; the difference is what the confidence threshold is applied to. Its absolute value does not test goodness of fit: E[statistic] is not (channels − parameters), so a χ2/DOF formed from the two numbers displayed beside each other is not a fit-quality measure and should not be read as one.

The per-row Currie limits include a decision threshold (Lc, the count above which a detection would be declared) and a detection limit (Ld, the activity that would reliably be detected). The combined deconvolution scan reports neither: doing so properly requires the null distribution to be calibrated by Monte Carlo at low counts rather than assumed, and that is not yet implemented. The deconvolution result is an upper limit, a central interval, or a predicted sensitivity — and it says which.
Uncertainties come from counting statistics, and from the finite statistics of a background reference where one is used. Detector-response and shielding-model uncertainties are not propagated.
